newsitem.title: USA: FUND VIEW - Scudder, Stevens global outlook.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Scudder, Stevens global outlook.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom's intitial public offering on Monday was a "watershed event" that may spur German investors to invest more in equities and pave the way for other European IPOs, said a managing director of the mutual fund firm Scudder, Stevens & Clark.

Nicholas Bratt, who manages or directs about 10 global funds for Scudder, said the Deutsche Telekom IPO was attractively priced and should trade higher in the weeks ahead. Germans historically have shied away from equity investments, but widespread advertising by Deutsche Telekom has lured many into the stock market for the first time.
"It's very important for the Germans to have a success here," Bratt told reporters while presenting his outlook for the global markets in 1997.

Bratt's bullishness on Deutsche Telekom extends to the European market as a whole. High unemployment and slow economic growth will burden most of Europe next year, but monetary policies may continue to ease and corporate profits should be strong, he said.

"We think the prospect for corporate profits is encouraging. Certainly the direction of growth of corporate profits is stronger than in the U.S. So we think that this will provide good support for European markets," Bratt said.
The one exception in Europe is Britain, where a fast-growing economy has raised the threat of higher inflation and prompted a rise in short-term interest rates, he said.

The markets have already factored in a victory by the British Labour Party in the next general election, which will take place next spring at the latest. The outcome should have no major impact on stocks in that country, he said.
Gary Johnson, director of fixed-income and derivative research for Scudder, said interest rate spreads have tightened so much this year that they may widen next year.
Any move by the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank or the Bank of Japan to increase rates could trigger "a fairly violent, rapid" reaction in interest rates in other countries.
"Usually bond investors assume they can get the return on the coupon. That may not be the case as spreads widen out," said Johnson, who helps manage Scudder's Global Bond Fund.
Some bond funds could even have negative returns, he said.

Bratt said he expected China's takeover of Hong Kong next year to proceed smoothly, which should bolster markets there and in Taiwan. Indeed, expectations of a smooth transition are behind strong gains this year, he said.
"There's an enormous desire not to lose face and to show the world that ... the Chinese can manage Hong Kong just as well," he said.

On a broad basis, he expected funds in Asia to redistribute their holdings, selling assets in those countries that have outperformed at a profit in favor of cheaper assets of those countries that have underperformed.
To be sure, Japan still has financial problems to work out, although it too has some attractive stocks, he said.
Debt denominated in local currencies in emerging markets is looking more attractive and, in U.S. dollars, could offer gains of about 10 percent, Johnson said.
"Our feeling is that the differentiation between emerging markets and investment-grade developed markets is going to erode," he said. "Eventually that distinction becomes meaningless."
